source.title: Sequenced-Replacement Sampling for Deep Learning
source.authors: Chiu-Man Ho; D. Park; Wei Yang; Yi Chang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares training procedures and reports test errors on natural image labels, but does not test memorization of random labels or most listed mechanisms.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for sequenced-replacement sampling (SRS), which are relevant to generalization but do not directly test a listed version. For V5, Table 3 compares batch sizes 64 and 128 for WRN and states that the difference is not significant. Cited results in the related-work section are not treated as this study's results.
record.test_reason: Table 3 directly compares batch sizes using held-out classification error at the same 200-epoch budget, bearing on V5. The main SRS experiments do not test the listed versions. The batch comparison does not establish that either size exceeds the workload-dependent threshold in V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors conclude that SRS combined with a longer initial high-learning-rate period improves CIFAR-100 accuracy and permits deeper WRNs to improve further, while slowing convergence without adding inference cost. They emphasize its compatibility with BN-after-addition residual units; their proposed exploration mechanism is an interpretation rather than a directly measured mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: SRS changes the sampling procedure by refilling the dataset with sequenced samples; the paper compares it with non-replacement sampling. Models use horizontal flips and random crops, dropout and weight decay in the stated WRN configuration.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset (CIFAR-10 versus CIFAR-100), residual-unit configuration, and learning-rate schedule affect the reported outcome. The authors state that SRS correlates better with the Wide ResNet “BN after addition” residual unit than with the original residual unit; an early learning-rate decay reduces the SRS result on CIFAR-100.

fits_no_version.finding: SRS improves reported CIFAR-100 error substantially for BN-after-addition WRN and more modestly for DenseNet; CIFAR-10 improvements are smaller. The DenseNet comparators are cited results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sequenced-replacement sampling can improve image-classification performance, with gains depending on dataset, architecture, and learning-rate schedule.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing WRN depth from 28 to 70 changes CIFAR-100 error from 19.42% to 19.72% without SRS and from 12.34% to 10.10% with SRS.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The generalization benefit of increasing network depth can depend on the sampling and training recipe.

record.problems: No random-label or training-error results are reported for the central claim. The batch-size comparison is limited to WRN on CIFAR-100 at sizes 64 and 128; the paper describes the difference as not significant but gives no uncertainty estimate for those values. Table 2 uncertainty is stated only for the paper's method as the median of five runs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional directly relevant rows left out. Other Table 2 baselines do not separately test an intervention or condition named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the comparison of held-out performance under random and natural labels.
Widening beyond the width required for zero training error; the depth comparison is not a width sweep.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and their tuning.

The workload-dependent batch threshold, batches above 128, language models, and whether longer training, learning-rate scaling with warmup, or normalization and regularization changes remove an established batch penalty.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and removal of dropout with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap correlations, and comparisons against other generalization measures.
Identification and removal of memorized examples followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The record's challenges verdict overstates the batch-size result: a null comparison between 64 and 128 does not contradict a claim explicitly conditioned on exceeding a workload-dependent threshold. States for rows linked to none are cannot_determine with respect to the listed versions, not judgments that their reported test errors are unreadable.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy under random versus natural labels.
Width sweep past the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks trained from scratch, and local-connectivity tests.
Language models, batch sizes beyond 128, and the effects of longer training or normalization and regularization changes on the batch-size penalty.
Dropout comparisons and its interaction with data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to generalization gaps.
Removing influential memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

relationships.condition: BN-after-addition WRN on CIFAR-100, ordinary sampling, batch sizes 64 versus 128, 200 epochs, identical original learning-rate schedule
relationships.reason: R9 and R10 report 18.38% versus 18.47% error, which the authors describe as no significant difference. This bounds the observed penalty in this interval; it does not challenge V5's conditional claim about batches beyond a workload-dependent threshold.
relationships.display_finding: Error changed from 18.38% to 18.47%, which the authors described as insignificant without providing uncertainty estimates or identifying a harmful batch threshold.
